nature-eco-198.title: How cities, farms and clearing reshape the water cycle
nature-eco-198.text: Pave a meadow, and the rain that once soaked into it runs off instead. Changes in how land is used and what covers it, such as cities, farm expansion and deforestation, alter the water cycle locally and regionally. They affect rainfall, evaporation, flooding, groundwater and how much fresh water is available. Compacted soils and paved surfaces reduce how much water soaks in and increase surface runoff. Clearing forests reduces local soil moisture, evaporation, rain and snow, and across a region it can shift temperatures and rainfall patterns. Dams can change natural river flows, lower water quality and destroy habitat for aquatic species. The effect can run the other way too. Trees help regulate the water cycle, reduce soil erosion and prevent runoff, so planting new forests can improve water management.

nature-eco-199.title: A warmer world, a stronger water cycle
nature-eco-199.text: Since at least 1980, the water cycle has been running harder. Water cycle intensification is this strengthening of the cycle, caused by human-driven global warming. Human-caused warming has visibly changed the global water cycle since the mid-20th century. The reason is simple: a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapour, and that changes both evaporation and rainfall. One result is that heavy rain events become even stronger. The effects spread widely. Intensification harms the availability of fresh water, and it affects the oceans, the ice sheets, the atmosphere and the moisture in soils. The IPCC's 2021 Sixth Assessment Report predicted that these changes will keep growing, both globally and region by region.

nature-eco-252.title: The ocean's carbon cycle: a source turned sink
nature-eco-252.text: Before the Industrial Revolution, the ocean released carbon dioxide to the air. Today it does the opposite, taking up a net 2.9 billion tonnes of carbon a year on average. The oceanic carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon among pools within the ocean, and between the ocean, the atmosphere, Earth's interior and the seafloor. It is central to the global carbon cycle and holds both inorganic carbon and organic carbon, the kind built by living things. Three main pumps carry carbon dioxide from the air into the ocean interior and spread it through the oceans. Altogether, the oceans take up around 25–31% of the carbon dioxide people emit. Temperature matters. Cold water dissolves more carbon dioxide, so warming seas take up less. Carbon also arrives by river: rivers deliver roughly equal amounts, about 0.4 gigatons of carbon a year each, of dissolved inorganic and organic carbon. Since 1970, dams have cut that delivery by an estimated 13%. The final exit is burial in sediments, the ocean's long-term carbon sink and its largest loss of carbon. About 90% of organic carbon burial happens on deltas, continental shelves and upper slopes.

nature-eco-248.title: Ocean acidification: the other carbon dioxide problem
nature-eco-248.text: Between 1950 and 2020, the average pH of the ocean surface fell from about 8.15 to 8.05. The pH scale measures acidity, and lower numbers mean more acidic. That small-looking drop means roughly 26% more hydrogen ions, the particles that make water acidic. Ocean acidification is this ongoing fall in the pH of Earth's ocean as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. Carbon dioxide from human activities is the main cause. Dissolved in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions that lower the pH. Seawater is still alkaline, the opposite of acidic, with a pH above 8. Acidification means it is becoming less so. The creatures most at risk build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate: mollusks, corals and others. Speed is the danger. Today's rate of change is far faster than in the geological past, too fast for organisms to adapt gradually. Acidification has happened before, during several mass extinctions, including the end-Permian and Cretaceous–Paleogene events. Combined with ocean warming, it harms marine life far more than either alone. Only cutting carbon dioxide emissions addresses the root cause, though removing carbon dioxide from the air would also help reverse it.

nature-eco-204.title: The biological pump: how plankton send carbon to the deep
nature-eco-204.text: Without the ocean's living pump, the air would hold about 400 parts per million more carbon dioxide than it does today. The biological pump is the ocean's living process of moving carbon from the air and from land runoff into the deep ocean and seafloor sediments. It starts in the sunlit surface layer, where phytoplankton build organic and inorganic carbon compounds. Their reach is enormous: marine phytoplankton perform half of all photosynthesis on Earth. Uneaten phytoplankton clump together and sink quickly out of the well-mixed surface layer. The faecal pellets of zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, sink with them. In this way the pump moves about 11 billion tonnes of carbon into the ocean interior each year. Large animals help. Whales and seals boost surface productivity by releasing nitrogen-rich fecal plumes, a role that was larger before industrial fishing cut their numbers. The pump may weaken in future. As the surface ocean warms and stratifies, separating into layers that mix less, nutrient supply and primary production may fall.

nature-eco-250.title: What ocean acidification could cost people
nature-eco-250.text: About one billion people depend wholly or partly on coral reefs for fishing, tourism and protection of their coasts. Ocean acidification threatens that, along with commercial fisheries, shellfish harvests and coastal tourism. Slower calcification, the building of shells and skeletons, means smaller, slower-growing reefs, and reefs support about 25% of marine life. Depending on how much carbon is emitted, future acidification may affect the livelihoods of some 470 to 870 million of the world's poorest people. Rich countries are exposed too. The US commercial fish catch in 2007 was worth $3.8 billion, and 73% of it came from shell-builders and their direct predators. In the United Kingdom, the direct potential loss is put at 14 to 28 percent of shellfish fishery output, about 23 to 88 million pounds. Arctic fisheries are at risk because acidification harms pteropods and brittle stars, creatures at the base of simple Arctic food webs.

nature-eco-271.title: The solubility pump: cold water drags carbon down
nature-eco-271.text: A cold sea holds more carbon dioxide than a warm one, and the ocean puts that fact to work. The solubility pump is a physical and chemical process that carries carbon, as dissolved inorganic carbon, from the ocean surface into its depths. It works because carbon dioxide dissolves better in cold water, and because deep water forms from cold, dense water at high latitudes, near the poles. That cold water sinks with its carbon. The return trip closes the loop. When deep water rises in warm equatorial seas, it releases carbon dioxide back to the air. About one third of human carbon dioxide emissions, approximately 2 gigatons of carbon per year, are believed to enter the ocean, driven mainly by this pump. That uptake slows global warming but causes ocean acidification. The pump may falter. Ocean warming, stronger layering of the water and slower thermohaline circulation could all weaken it. Thermohaline circulation is the slow, deep movement of ocean water driven by differences in temperature and saltiness. The pump's living counterpart is the biological pump.

nature-es-092.title: Erosion control: keeping soil in place with plants
nature-es-092.text: New Deal programs in the United States planted 18,000 miles of tree and shrub belts to break the wind, from North Dakota to Texas, to fight soil erosion. Erosion control is the set of practices that prevent or repair soil erosion, chiefly by keeping land covered with plants. Increasing plant cover is the most effective known way to prevent erosion by both wind and water. Terracing, cutting slopes into level steps, is a highly effective method practiced for thousands of years around the world. Such belts along fields also improve growing conditions around the crops, shelter birds and store carbon. Mixed cropping, {{ref:nature-nbs-276}} and leaving crop residues on the field under {{ref:nature-nbs-291}} all reduce erosion. {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, which mixes crops with trees, works especially well in rainy tropical climates. On coasts, the roots of the trees covered in {{ref:nature-eco-410}} slow water, trap sediment and bind soils. Good erosion control manages surface runoff and helps prevent water pollution, the loss of soil and habitat, and damage to property.

nature-eco-262.title: Managing soil carbon: farming as a climate tool
nature-eco-262.text: In the Netherlands, East Anglia and Florida, drained and tilled peat soils have sunk severely as their carbon oxidized. Managing soil carbon means using land in ways that keep or add carbon to soil. It matters because the exchange of carbon between soil and atmosphere is a major part of the global carbon cycle. Humans and farming systems are now the biggest influence on how soil carbon varies. Deforestation, fire, tillage, meaning plowing and similar working of the soil, and drainage all cause losses. Adding carbon brings co-benefits: less erosion, higher productivity, cleaner waterways and soil that holds water better. Farming practices that store carbon in soils, covered in {{ref:nature-nbs-226}}, are a land-based way to remove carbon dioxide from the air. Selling that storage is tricky, though. Soil carbon offsets can be hard to verify, because measurements depend on how deep the samples are taken.

nature-eco-246.title: Nutrient trading: paying the cheapest cleaner
nature-eco-246.text: Two polluters on the same river can face very different bills to cut the same pollutant. Nutrient trading puts that gap to work. It is one form of {{ref:nature-pol-287}}, a market-based policy tool in which sources swap credits for cutting nutrient pollution. Sources that can cut pollution cheaply sell reduction credits voluntarily to sources for which control is expensive. The underlying principle is that the polluter pays, usually backed by a rule requiring participation. A 2013 Forest Trends report found three kinds of funders. Some benefit from protecting a watershed, some are polluters offsetting their impacts, and some are public good payers such as governments and NGOs, the non-governmental organizations. As of 2013, payments were overwhelmingly started by that last group.

nature-eco-273.title: The sulfur cycle: an element that trades electrons
nature-eco-273.text: Sulfur is found in many proteins, so every living thing needs it. The sulfur cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves sulfur between rocks, waterways and living things. It runs through changes in sulfur's oxidation state, a count of how many electrons an atom has given up or gained. That state ranges from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides. The steps include breaking down organic sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, oxidizing sulfide to sulfate, and reducing sulfate back to sulfide. Microbes that oxidize sulfide often use the energy to fix carbon dioxide, building it into living matter. Sulfur compounds can also serve in cellular respiration. Earth's main sulfur sink is the sulfate dissolved in the oceans. In the seabed, sulfate is used to break down buried organic matter and methane. Deeper down, where the sulfate runs out, methane production takes over. Sulfur also takes part in forming fossil fuels and most metal ore deposits.

nature-eco-256.title: Permafrost: the Arctic's frozen carbon vault
nature-eco-256.text: Permafrost soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of the organic carbon in the world's soils. Permafrost is ground that stays below 0 °C for at least two years in a row. The permafrost, or Arctic, carbon cycle is the part of the global carbon cycle that moves carbon between frozen soils, plants and microbes, the atmosphere and back. The northern circumpolar permafrost region alone holds around 1,460–1,600 Pg, or petagrams, of organic carbon in its soils. That is more than double the carbon now in the atmosphere. The carbon is old: radiocarbon dating shows it is often thousands of years old. It got there slowly. Wind and rivers dropped sediment, peat built up, and as the ground surface rose, the buried layers froze into the permafrost with their carbon locked inside. Early research often overlooked this huge store, but attention has grown enormously since the 2000s. What happens when it thaws is the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-257}}.

nature-eco-241.title: Net ecosystem production: the carbon an ecosystem keeps
nature-eco-241.text: Net ecosystem production is the carbon an ecosystem has left after every living thing in it has respired. Formally, it is gross primary production minus all the respiration in an ecosystem, by plants, animals and microbes. It is given as mass of carbon per area per time, such as grams of carbon per square meter per year. The leftover carbon can be stored as biomass, buried in sediments or soils, or exported to another system. It can also be burned, or broken down by sunlight, and so turned back into carbon dioxide. Net primary production is different: it subtracts only the plants' own respiration, not that of animals and microbes. The measure has practical uses. It is one of the main factors directly linked to methane emissions from wetlands.

nature-eco-191.title: The light-dependent reactions: catching sunlight
nature-eco-191.text: Photosynthesis begins when a molecule of chlorophyll, the green pigment of plants, absorbs a photon, a particle of light. These light-dependent reactions are the first stage of photosynthesis, making the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. In plants they take place in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts. The absorbed photon makes chlorophyll lose an electron. The electron travels down a chain of molecules and ends up turning NADP into NADPH. Chlorophyll regains its electron when water is split, which releases oxygen.

nature-eco-192.title: The Calvin cycle: building sugar from air
nature-eco-192.text: At Berkeley in the late 1940s, Melvin Calvin and colleagues worked out how plants build sugar from air. Calvin won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The Calvin cycle is the light-independent stage of photosynthesis. In it the enzyme RuBisCO, a protein that speeds the reaction, captures carbon dioxide from the air and builds it into sugars. The power comes from the ATP and NADPH made by the light-dependent reactions. The products are carbohydrates such as glucose. These simple sugars become cellulose, building blocks for fats and proteins, or fuel for respiration.

nature-eco-193.title: Carbon concentrating mechanisms: photosynthesis in the heat
nature-eco-193.text: On a hot, dry day a plant faces a dilemma. Closing its stomata saves water, but the carbon dioxide inside the leaf then falls and a wasteful process called photorespiration rises. Carbon concentrating mechanisms are ways some plants and algae raise the carbon dioxide level around RuBisCO so photosynthesis keeps working. C4 plants first fix carbon dioxide into a four-carbon acid using the enzyme PEP carboxylase. C4 and CAM plants avoid photorespiration this way, raising their yield in some high-energy environments. Cyanobacteria concentrate carbon dioxide inside structures called carboxysomes.

nature-eco-195.title: What holds photosynthesis back
nature-eco-195.text: Shade from neighbouring plants is a major brake on photosynthesis. Total photosynthesis is limited by environmental factors: light, leaf area, carbon dioxide supply, water and temperature. Carbon dioxide shows how the limits work. As its concentration rises, sugar production rises, until some other factor becomes the limit. Part of the story lies in RuBisCO, the enzyme that captures carbon. It binds both carbon dioxide and oxygen, and it fixes carbon dioxide when carbon dioxide concentration is high.

nature-eco-194.title: Photosynthetic efficiency: plants versus solar panels
nature-eco-194.text: A typical plant turns only 3–6% of the light it receives into chemical energy. That share is its photosynthetic efficiency. It varies with the colour and intensity of light, temperature and carbon dioxide level, ranging from 0.1% to 8%. Mass-produced solar panels do better, converting light to electricity at about 6–20%, and laboratory devices exceed 40%. Scientists study photosynthesis partly in the hope of breeding plants with higher yields.

nature-eco-278.title: Agricultural runoff: farm chemicals on the move
nature-eco-278.text: Spray a field just before heavy rain, and the chemicals may end up in the nearest stream. Agricultural runoff is water flowing off farmland that carries chemicals such as nitrates, phosphates, pesticides and herbicides. It happens when chemicals are overused or applied just before heavy rain. Either way, farm chemicals are wasted and downstream ecosystems are threatened. Nitrate fertilizer is especially easily lost, because it is highly soluble and is repelled by negatively charged clay. Concentrated runoff from farms can cause dead zones in large water bodies.

nature-eco-276.title: Two ways a storm sets water running
nature-eco-276.text: Surface runoff is generated in distinct ways. Infiltration excess, or Hortonian, overland flow starts when rain falls faster than the soil can soak it up. It is common in dry regions with intense rain and sealed soils, and in paved urban areas. Saturation excess, or Dunne, runoff happens when rain keeps falling on soil that is already full of water. The wetter the soil before a storm, the sooner it saturates and runoff begins. Some water takes a hidden route. It soaks in upslope, flows sideways through the soil and re-emerges near a channel, which is called subsurface return flow, or throughflow.

nature-eco-279.title: Taming runoff, from medieval fields to city drains
nature-eco-279.text: Since medieval times, farmers have protected their soil by contour farming, plowing across slopes rather than down them. Runoff mitigation combines controls on how land is used, erosion controls, flood control and chemical handling rules to reduce the harm runoff causes. Construction sites use straw bales, silt fences and work scheduled for drier months to slow runoff. Holding ponds, also called detention basins, buffer peak river flows. In the United States, the federal law described in {{ref:nature-pol-155}} requires urban local governments to run programs for managing storm runoff, under discharge permits.

nature-eco-277.title: Urban runoff: rain that never meets the soil
nature-eco-277.text: Rain that falls on a road, a parking lot or a roof cannot soak in. Urban runoff is the surface runoff that hard surfaces like these create, from rain, landscape watering and car washing. Instead of filtering through soil, polluted rainwater flows to storm drains. Most municipal storm sewers then discharge it untreated into streams, rivers and bays. Because more water stays on the surface, the water table drops and floods become more common. Many towns respond with building codes, such as narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, that let more water soak in.

nature-eco-172.title: Timber buildings: storing forest carbon in cities
nature-eco-172.text: A wooden building can keep hold of carbon a tree once pulled from the air. Buildings made of mass timber, large structural pieces of solid wood, can therefore act as artificial carbon sinks. Replacing steel and concrete with timber could store between 10 million and close to 700 million tons of carbon a year, depending on the scenario. The benefit has conditions. The forests must be sustainably managed, and the wood must be reused or preserved when buildings are demolished. Fast-growing plant materials such as bamboo, straw or hempcrete can add further storage.

nature-eco-546.title: Coastal eutrophication: why nitrogen rules the sea
nature-eco-546.text: Over the last century, rivers' yearly delivery to the oceans rose from 19 to 37 megatonnes of nitrogen and from 2 to 4 megatonnes of phosphorus. Coastal eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of coastal seas, where nitrogen is usually the main culprit. In fresh water, phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient, the one in shortest supply that caps growth. In coastal waters, nitrogen usually is. So nitrogen levels matter more than phosphorus for controlling eutrophication in salt water. The pressure on each coast varies with land activities in its catchment, the land that drains into it. It also depends on how well the setting dilutes nutrients and exchanges oxygen.

nature-eco-219.title: Harmful algal blooms: when green water turns toxic
nature-eco-219.text: Some algal blooms do more than starve a lake of oxygen. Harmful algal blooms are dense growths of algae, often caused by eutrophication, that are toxic to plants and animals. When the algae die or are eaten, they release nerve and liver toxins that can kill animals and may threaten humans. The toxins can reach people through shellfish, causing shellfish poisoning. In fresh water, the culprits are commonly cyanobacteria that fix their own nitrogen. They are favoured when nitrogen runs short but phosphorus keeps pouring in.

nature-eco-220.title: The economic bill for murky, smelly water
nature-eco-220.text: Murky water costs money to clean. Eutrophication and harmful algal blooms impose economic costs through dearer water treatment, lost fishing and shellfish harvests, and lower tourism income. Drinking water plants must also deal with colour and smell problems. Tourism suffers because the water looks less attractive and is less safe, thanks to bacteria from decomposition. Could a little extra fertility pay? In principle, controlled eutrophication could raise fishery output and community income. It is not currently recommended, because damage can set in quickly.

nature-eco-218.title: Natural eutrophication: lakes grow richer with age
nature-eco-218.text: Lakes naturally grow more productive as they age. Natural eutrophication is this slow enrichment of waters by the gradual build-up of sediment and nutrients. It usually comes from dissolved phosphate minerals and dead plant matter collecting in the water. Climate, geology and other outside influences also regulate how productive a lake naturally is.

nature-eco-224.title: Nutrient bioextraction: oysters and kelp as water cleaners
nature-eco-224.text: Several studies show that oysters and mussels can greatly lower nitrogen levels in estuaries. Nutrient bioextraction is farming and harvesting shellfish and seaweed to remove nitrogen and other nutrients from natural waters. Seaweeds such as kelp absorb both phosphorus and nitrogen, helping clean polluted waters. The idea has an economic angle. If oysters keep nitrogen below legal thresholds, they spare polluters the compliance costs they would otherwise face. So nitrogen removal by reefs of oysters could benefit polluters facing nitrogen limits, much as nutrient trading does.

nature-eco-223.title: Preventing eutrophication at the source
nature-eco-223.text: The surest way to stop a lake being overfed is to stop feeding it. Eutrophication is prevented mainly by cutting nutrient pollution from sewage and from farming. Sewage treatment plants can be upgraded for biological nutrient removal, so they discharge much less nitrogen and phosphorus. That matters because even good standard treatment leaves substantial nitrogen in the treated water most sewage plants release. Farmers are advised to apply fertilizer in the right amount, at the right time, with the right method and placement. The UN's goal for the oceans, described in {{ref:nature-gov-027}}, targets a significant cut in marine nutrient pollution from land by 2025.

nature-eco-225.title: Reversing eutrophication: why lakes recover slowly
nature-eco-225.text: Stopping the flow of nutrients into a lake does not clean it overnight. Reversing eutrophication starts with reducing nutrient inputs, but recovery can take a long time, mainly because nutrients stored in sediments keep being released. Cutting inputs may not be enough. A water body can have several stable but very different states, so restoration may need more. One option is adding phosphate-binding materials such as alum to lock up phosphorus. Removal at the source can be thorough: Finnish phosphorus removal from the mid-1970s reached 90% removal efficiency.
